Seized by Parliamentarians at Hamsterley in July 1644 while wearing his Mass vestments, he was carried to London and committed to Newgate with his friend John Duckett, a secular priest. At the Old Bailey both admitted their priesthood, were condemned, and were executed together on 7 September. Stonyhurst holds a relic of Corbie, and his letters survive in Foley's records of the English Jesuit province.
chesnut-diary-from-dixie:
Mary Chesnut kept her famous diary inside the Confederate elite during the Civil War. She revised it in the 1880s, and it was published in 1905 as A Diary from Dixie. Her husband was a Confederate senator and general, so she heard everything.

Chesnut records Charleston drawing rooms, Richmond gossip, and the war news reaching anxious families. She is witty about generals, sharp about slavery, and honest about dread as defeat nears. Unlike most diaries, hers reads like a novel, with scenes and dialogue rebuilt by a gifted writer. Many call it the most literary diary of the Civil War.

doe-osti-3912523-nsls-ii-radioactive-sam: Handling radioactive samples at a synchrotron takes careful math first. Dos Santos Augusto ran radiation field calculations for NSLS-II's radioactive samples using FLUKA, a particle-transport code. The numbers map where radiation goes so shielding and procedures keep people safe.
evangeline-a-tale-of-acadie:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's Evangeline, A Tale of Acadie opens in the forest primeval, among murmuring pines and hemlocks standing like Druids of eld. Below them once stood Grand-Pre, the Acadian village the British destroyed in 1755. Evangeline Bellefontaine and Gabriel Lajeunesse are betrothed on the very eve of the expulsion.

The poem follows Evangeline's lifelong search down the Mississippi and across America, through churchyards and towns, always just missing Gabriel, until she finds him dying in a Philadelphia almshouse. Longfellow wrote in hexameters learned from Homer and Goethe. Published in 1847, the poem made the Acadian tragedy famous worldwide and fixed Longfellow as America's household poet for a century.
field-and-hedgerow-being-the-last-essays:
Richard Jefferies's Field and Hedgerow gathers his last essays, collected by his widow after his death. The essays first appeared in the Fortnightly Review, the Manchester Guardian, the Pall Mall Gazette, the Standard, Longman's Magazine and other periodicals of the day.

Contents include Hours of Spring, The July Grass, Winds of Heaven, Swallow-Time, Walks in the Wheat-Fields, Field Words and Ways, Cottage Ideas, and Summer in Somerset. Jefferies writes of Sussex, deer-parks, old villages and birds' nests with the close observation that made him famous. Readers who love English nature writing will find Field and Hedgerow a fitting, autumnal close to his work.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrackenEddie_Br: nsia-BrackenEddie Bracken Eddie: the made public government document on Eddie Bracken, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, of the files. From the archive shelves, for readers.

The writer then turns to business: efforts to persuade David Belin to support a new investigation. Belin had served on the Warren Commission staff. The author's name cannot be recovered, so the letter survives as an unsigned snapshot of researchers lobbying for a reopened inquiry in 1976.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-YatesDixie_Yate: An FBI memo from 1975 records information Dixie Yates gave the Dallas office by telephone about the JFK assassination. Twelve years after the shooting, citizens still called in tips and memories. The bureau still wrote them down. The Yates memo is a late entry in a file that never fully closed, showing how long the assassination kept generating new paper.
indiscretions-of-archie:
P. G. Wodehouse set his farce Indiscretions of Archie in a grand New York hotel, where a penniless Englishman has married the owner's daughter. Archie Moffam wed Lucille Brewster for love, with neither money nor a job to offer. Daniel Brewster, the hotel proprietor and father-in-law, has never forgiven Archie for once criticizing his hotel. George H. Doran published the book in 1921.

Chapters chain Archie's blundering good deeds into fresh disasters for the Brewster household. He hunts for work, poses as an artist's model, and tangles with a bomb plot scare. Brother Bill's romance, a sausage seller, and young Washy finding fame fill the middle episodes. Reggie, Looney Biddle, and Mr. Connolly each get a turn in the machinery. The Wigmore Venus, a statue with a past, drives the closing mix-ups. Wodehouse keeps every scrape light, fast, and forgiven by the final page, in his early manner.
keeping-up-with-lizzie:
Keeping Up with Lizzie is Irving Bacheller's novel of a small town turned upside down, published by Harper in March 1911. W. L. Jacobs illustrated it, and Bacheller dedicates it to Mr. Onedear. In Pointview, the tradesmen form a sort of board of assessors. Lizzie, newly back from travel abroad, has met a queen and gained an accent and a fiancé.

Her return sets off a race of spending and showing off among her old neighbors. The ham war and flying visits fill the middle chapters. The Honorable Socrates Potter, the town's shrewd lawyer, finally catches up with Lizzie in the last. Bacheller satirizes small-town pride through one girl's rise and everyone's scramble to match it.
lady-connie:
Mrs. Humphry Ward published her novel Lady Connie in 1916. Albert Sterner drew its pictures. The book runs in three parts and nineteen chapters.

Constance, called Connie, stands at the center of the story. A picture caption shows her entranced by music at a tea party. Another shows her with Falloden at her feet under a plane tree. Ward mixes romance with serious talk about duty and character. Readers who like her thoughtful social novels will find that blend here. Ward's heroines often face a test of conscience. Connie's story follows that pattern within Oxford and country house settings.
literary-hearthstones-of-dixie:
La Salle Corbell Pickett published this tour of Southern literary homes in 1912. J. B. Lippincott issued it with portraits and illustrations. Pickett also wrote Pickett and His Men and Jinny. Her foreword finds fires still glowing on old hearthstones.

Southern writers once welcomed friends at those firesides, she writes. Gifted pens there gave voice to readers' own unspoken thoughts. The builders of those shrines have passed from the world. Pickett tends their memory for a later generation of readers. Four feet on the fender recalled talks with gifted friends. Heart's-blood pens, Pickett writes, voiced readers' own flaming thoughts.
love-letters-of-a-rookie-to-julie:
Love Letters of a Rookie to Julie is a comic war book by Barney Stone. Stone served with Headquarters Company, 119th Field Artillery, in France. The book, copyrighted in 1919, prints his letters home to Julie. Gordon Ross drew the funny pictures that go with them.

The rookie writes in cheerful, mangled spelling from camp and trench. He tells of the train ride, the farewell at Julie's flat, and army food. His slang and mix-ups carry the humor of a green soldier. Real affection for Julie runs under all the jokes. The letters give a light, human view of the American doughboy.
marie:
Marie is a story by Laura E. Richards, published in 1894. Richards also wrote Captain January and Queen Hildegarde. Her Marie has walked nearly the whole day as the sun sinks. Long rays rest on farmhouse windows and tree-tops like fiddle-bows.

Marie thinks in music, and hugs her treasure close as a baby. She has run away from the troupe she traveled with. The face of 'Le Boss' still makes her shiver in memory. Ahead lies a New England village, a kind family, and a new life. Chapters promise courtship, wedlock, and a vita nuova — a new life. Richards tells it with her usual warmth and grace.
mary-marie:
Eleanor H. Porter published Mary Marie in 1920. Helen Mason Grose drew the pictures for the book. A short preface says it will explain things at the start.

The heroine tells her own tale, from the words I Am Born. Nurse Sarah's story comes next, then the break in the home. Some chapters call her Mary, some Marie, and some both at once. That split name frames her search for which self is the real one. A test and a true love story wait near the end. Porter lets the girl's own voice carry both grief and hope.
mince-pie:
Christopher Morley collected these humorous sketches from the newspapers where they first appeared. Most ran in the Philadelphia Evening Public Ledger. Others came from The Bookman, the Boston Evening Transcript, Life, and The Smart Set. His instructions order the book to be read in bed, and never from a borrowed copy.

Morley calls the pieces trifles and offers no excuse for prolonging their existence. He hopes a copy on the bedside shelf may pave the way to easy slumber. The sketches include a mock account of a president traveling abroad. Morley's light essays show the daily newspaper humor column at its most genial.
mischievous-maid-faynie:
Laura Jean Libbey published this dime-novel romance in an author's special edition in 1899. The story opens during a terrible New York blizzard. Snow buries Broadway, cable cars stall, and two handsome young men breast the storm together. Strangers take them for twin brothers, but they are only cousins.

One cousin is Clinton Kendale, the actor everyone calls the rage of New York. The other is Lester Armstrong, an assistant cashier with no great hopes. Libbey wrote popular romances like Ione and Parted by Fate for working readers. Snow, stage fame, and a mischievous maid drive this tale of love and mistaken standing.
miss-dexie:
Stanford Eveleth published this Canadian novel at Toronto in 1895. He subtitles it A Romance of the Provinces. The introduction is dated 1864, in wartime. News of the American Civil War fills a New England town with grief and argument, as casualty lists grow daily.

Wives' and mothers' faces whiten as men hurry to telegraph offices for news. Eveleth, published by William Briggs with agents in Montreal and Halifax, wrote for readers across the young Dominion. His romance crosses the border in feeling: Canadians watching a neighboring republic tear itself apart. The provinces' own loyalties and families carry the story forward.
mother-s-remedies-over-one-thousand-trie:
Dr. Thomas Jefferson Ritter compiled this vast book of home cures from mothers across the United States and Canada. Its title promises over one thousand tried and tested remedies. The transcriber's notes warn modern readers first. Recipes call for kerosene, turpentine, lead, lye, strychnine, arsenic, mercury, opium, and cocaine.

Poultices appear in hundreds of recipes, and keeping the bowels open in nearly fifteen hundred. The transcriber calls the book a window into mothers' terror when a child fell ill. Doctors of the era could often offer little more. As social history, the volume is unmatched; as medicine, it belongs firmly to its time.
nasa-tm-19680020515-high-temperature-cre:
Robert J. Buzzard of Lewis Research Center measured creep-rupture strength in a tungsten and uranium dioxide cermet for this 1968 report. The material mixes equal volumes of tungsten and uranium dioxide. It was made by roll compaction of tungsten-coated uranium dioxide particles, then clad with tungsten.

Tests ran at very high temperatures under steady stress until samples broke. Rupture lives ranged from about one hour to hundreds of hours, depending on heat and load. Buzzard used the Manson-Haferd parameter to predict longer-term behavior and creep stages. He also examined what role the uranium dioxide plays in the failure process. The tungsten phase seemed to control strength and ductility.
podcast-tuckercarlson-r_Vt_Lo5SiE:
Independent researcher Ian Carroll joins Tucker Carlson to revisit America's deadliest mass shooting, the 2017 Las Vegas attack. Carroll built a following by questioning official stories in viral videos. Here he airs the unanswered questions he says authorities do not want asked.

Carroll walks through the timeline gaps, witness accounts, and evidence disputes in the case. He asks why the motive was never settled in public. Carlson, who has covered the story's odd turns before, presses for what a real inquiry would need. Questioning viewers get a citizen's probe into a case that still unsettles the country.
poems-c-1790-wherein-it-is-attempted-to-:
London readers in 1790 could buy an anonymous volume whose title page promises poems attempting to describe certain views of nature and of rustic manners. To show how the same circumstances affect different characters differently. Printed for J. Johnson in St. Paul's Churchyard, the book carries no author's name, only its program: close observation of country life, rendered in verse, with an eye on human variety.

The opening poem, A Winter Day, begins before dawn with the cock crowing among his hens. Then follows the laboring hind who dreams of gold from next year's crop and wakes to find himself the same poor man. Detail piles up lovingly: straw beds, home-spun coverings, the smothered fire blown back to life. The volume belongs to the late-century turn toward realistic rural poetry that prepared the way for Wordsworth and Clare.
sir-gibbie:
George MacDonald wrote this Scots novel around a small, saintly boy called Gibbie. Contents run through thirty-one chapters, from The Earring and Sir George to Mistress Croale and The Parlour. A glossary of broad Scots, added by the electronic text's maker, stands at the end to help with the dialogue.

Later heads promise Gibbie adrift, a barn refuge, Donal Grant, apprenticeship, and secret service. MacDonald sets a child of pure heart among drunks, lairds, and gamekeepers in the Scottish hills. Love and quiet goodness, not force, carry Gibbie through a hard world that keeps misreading him.
sister-carrie:
Theodore Dreiser published this novel with Doubleday, Page in New York in 1900 and dedicated it to his friend Arthur Henry. A copied hand-written note at the front thanks a Mr. Norris for early, full approval of the story in draft. Dreiser credits that backing for the book reaching print so soon.

Carrie, a young woman from the country, rides toward Chicago's lights in the tale that follows. Work, hunger, the stage, and kept luxury test her in turn. Dreiser's first novel shocked its age with a heroine who rises by paths that polite fiction condemned, and it still anchors talk on American realism.
t-mann-buddenbrooks-verfall-einer-famili:
Four generations of Luebeck merchants rise and fall in Buddenbrooks, given here in Mann's original German as Buddenbrooks: Verfall einer Familie. Published in 1901, the novel made its twenty-six-year-old author world-famous. Its subtitle announces the theme: the decline of a family, tracked across a century of trade.

In Mann's own language, the prose shows the irony and music that translation can only suggest. Business ledgers and family Bibles record christenings, marriages, failures, and deaths in equal detail. Vitality ebbs from commerce into art as the generations pass. The book eventually carried its author to the Nobel Prize. German readers still meet it young and return to it for life.
the-arte-of-english-poesie:
Printed at London by Richard Field in the Blackfriars in 1589, The Arte of English Poesie divides its craft into three books: of poets and poetry, of proportion, and of ornament. No author's name stands on the title page. A shield shows a hand coming out of a cloud and gripping an anchor twined with vine.

Field the printer addresses the book to Sir William Cecil, Lord Burghley, high treasurer of England. He admits the book came to his hands with its bare title only, no author and no address. Many passages showed it was meant for the Queen's own pastime and service, he says, which made him doubt whether he should present it to any other person at all.
the-awakening-of-helena-richie:
Margaret Deland dated her novel May 12, 1906, and linked it to her earlier Dr Lavendar's People. Dr Lavendar drives his horse Goliath up a muddy hill in Old Chester to call on old Benjamin Wright. He dislikes the duty but tells his small dog Daniel that pastoral calls are not about liking.

On the way home he passes the Stuffed Animal House, once owned by a taxidermist, where Mrs Frederick Richie watches his buggy go by. Wright, lonely and sharp-tongued, has not spoken to his only son Samuel for more than thirty years. Small-town duty, old quarrels, and a widow's watchful life set the scene.
the-german-classics-of-the-nineteenth-an: Kuno Francke edited The German Classics, a twenty-volume set of German masterworks in English dress, and this first volume was printed at Albany in 1913. Only the front matter and start of contents are present here. The volume opens with a life of Goethe, then his poems in versions by Charles Wharton Stork and E. A. Bowring, among them Prometheus and The Heathrose. No full work is included in this portion, so the texts cannot be told from these opening pages alone.
the-lesser-bourgeoisie:
Honore de Balzac dedicated his novel of the Paris middle classes to Constance-Victoire in a playful letter. He says Moliere left a few scraps of clay unused when he built Tartuffe, and Balzac kneaded those scraps into a modern hypocrite. Katharine Prescott Wormeley translated the book into English, as its title page states.

Part one follows the lesser bourgeois of Paris, opening at the tourniquet Saint-Jean, a narrow passage into the city. Balzac studies clerks, widows, and place seekers who scheme for small gains and thin respect. His comedy stays sharp about money, rank, and self deception in a crowded capital.
the-marquis-of-lossie: George MacDonald wrote The Marquis of Lossie. Only the title page and contents are present, so the novel does not appear. The forty-four chapter titles begin in a stable-yard and a library, introduce Miss Horn, a horse named Kelpie, Lizzy Findlay, and Mr. Crathie, then travel: Voyage to London, London Streets, The Tempest, and Kelpie in London. Later titles include The Schoolmaster, The Preacher, The Portrait, An Evil Omen, A Quarrel, The Two Daimons, Lies, An Old Enemy, and a final chapter, The Mind of the Author.
the-pigeon-pie: Charlotte M. Yonge's The Pigeon Pie is shown here in the new edition published by A. R. Mowbray and Co. in 1905. The firm had offices in Oxford and London. Here only the title page and the start of the contents appear, so the story itself is absent. The contents list chapters by number and page only, Chapter I at page 1 and Chapter V at page 62. A sibling record of the same 1905 edition carries the same front matter and then goes on into the first chapter.
the-poetical-works-of-oliver-wendell-hol:
Earlier Poems, 1830 to 1836, form the opening section of The Poetical Works of Oliver Wendell Holmes in the 1893 three-volume set. A contents list names Old Ironsides, The Last Leaf, and The Cambridge Churchyard. It also names To an Insect, The Dilemma, My Aunt, The Dorchester Giant, and The Comet. The Music-Grinders, The September Gale, and The Last Reader follow, closing with Poetry: A Metrical Essay.

Before them stands a short verse address to his readers. Holmes asks not to be blamed for sparing their patience many a trivial verse. The earlier poems once shared a welcome, and the better may shield the worse. Some readers, he admits, may find a freshness in the ruder songs that newer work has lost. The lines turn on his own ageing. When those poems were written his locks were brown; the ones he writes now belong to autumn.
the-prairie:
James Fenimore Cooper's The Prairie is framed by a contents list of thirty-four chapters and two introductions. An opening note states that the novel was the third in order of Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales. It first appeared in 1827. The note begins a short account of the book's place in the series before the tale itself starts.

Readers who know the series will place the story from that note alone. The prairie setting carries the Leatherstocking figure west, far from the forests of the earlier tales. The bare chapter numbers in the contents give no hint of scenes or persons. All the weight of the opening falls on the introductions, which set out the book's standing in Cooper's long frontier sequence.
the-princess-and-curdie: George MacDonald's The Princess and Curdie is shown through its contents and the bare heading of Chapter 1. The chapters themselves are not on view. Thirty-five chapters are listed, opening with The Mountain, The White Pigeon, and The Mistress of the Silver Moon. Curdie's father and mother, the miners, and the emerald follow. Middle titles include Curdie's Mission, Lina, The Dogs of Gwyntystorm, and The King's Kitchen. The Lord Chamberlain, Dr. Kelman, and The Prophecy lead toward The Avengers, The Sacrifice, The Battle, and Judgement.
the-spanish-tragedie: Thomas Kyd's revenge tragedy, dated 1587, appears in a text based on the earliest extant edition. John Matthews Manly edited it in 1897. A transcriber's note explains choices among editions and the exclusion of passages once supposed to be by Ben Jonson. The pages present here carry that note and the old title. The title promises the lamentable end of Don Horatio and Bel-imperia. A cast list begins with the ghost of Andrea, so the play itself does not appear.
the-story-of-jessie:
Mabel Quiller-Couch wrote this children's story in twelve chapters. The chapters begin with a letter for Sunnyside Cottage. Jessie's arrival and happy days follow. A journey and a new home come next. A final return to Springbrook closes the book. Chapter one opens in the Dawsons' kitchen. Thomas Dawson is busy there. He tries to make the kettle boil. He clears the fire so he can make a piece of toast.

Thomas has already tidied the grate. He has swept the floor too. He stands with the loaf in one hand. He is about to cut a slice. His eye wanders down the dewy, sunny garden. Every tree and bush shows the first green film on its brown branches. The spring morning prepares the cottage. The letter and the child of the title are on their way.
valerie:
Captain Frederick Marryat's novel Valerie, dated 1848, carries a preface that tells how the book was made. On August 10, 1845, Marryat wrote to a lady friend urging her to write her confessions, which he offered to publish. He had notes on the early life of a Frenchwoman, cast adrift at seventeen, and wanted to work her story together with the lady's own. Washington Irving, the preface says, had once wished to join in the same plan.

The lady declined, and the tale went ahead without her. It ran in the New Monthly in 1846 and 1847 under Marryat's hand for its first eleven chapters, as Mademoiselle Virginie. When it became a book called Valerie, another hand added the closing pages after his death. Readers get a French heroine's life story with an unusual birth: part magazine serial, part posthumous finish, explained frankly at the front.
winston-of-the-prairie: The front pages here give the title page and a partial contents list for Harold Bindloss's Winston of the Prairie, printed in 1907, with no story text present. W. Herbert Dunton drew the pictures. The frontispiece shows a man on foot urging a team through powdery snow drifts. The contents open with Rancher Winston and Lance Courthorne. A trooper's quarrel and Miss Barrington's homecoming follow. Winston comes to Silverdale, and Courthorne disappears, in the list. A promise by Maud Barrington and plowing fill later titles.
